answer.exemplar: The integrand is unbounded at the interior point x = 1, so the integral is improper and must be split into the integral from 0 to 1 and the integral from 1 to 2 of (x-1)^(-2) dx. Therefore the integral diverges to plus infinity, and the finite endpoint difference the student computed ignores the singularity entirely.

questions.explanation: An interior singularity forces the integral to be split at x = 1, and each side then diverges because negative 1 over (x-1) blows up there. Evaluating only at the endpoints skips the infinite contribution near the pole.

answer.exemplar: Both integrands tend to zero, but tending to zero is only necessary, not sufficient, for an integral to converge. answer.exemplar: The partial integral is x^(1-p) over (1-p) evaluated from 1 to b, namely (b^(1-p) - 1)/(1-p), and its limit as b grows depends on the sign of 1 - p. If 1 - p is negative, then b^(1-p) tends to zero and the limit is the finite value 1/(p-1). If 1 - p is zero, the antiderivative is ln b and the limit is infinite. questions.explanation: The limit of b^(1-p) is zero exactly when p exceeds 1, which is precisely the condition for a finite limit of the partial integral. The borderline p = 1 gives the logarithmically divergent harmonic integral.

options.misconception: judges convergence by the ease of differentiating the antiderivative

options.text: The exponent 0 gives a divergent integral, but only because the area under a constant is hard to compute
options.misconception: misattributes a divergence to computational difficulty

options.text: An exponent of 0 makes the integrand equal to 1, whose integral over an infinite interval plainly diverges

questions.explanation: With p = 0 the integrand is 1, and the area under a constant 1 over an infinite interval is infinite. The convergence condition p above 1 excludes p = 0 immediately, and the least admissible integer is 2.
questions.hint: Check what the integrand looks like when the exponent is zero.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Logarithmic divergence at infinity
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a sketch of unbounded logarithmic growth
questions.stem: A plot shows the curve of ln b for b at least 1 rising without ever flattening, and a horizontal line drawn well above part of the curve. What does the sketch show about the improper integral?

options.text: The curve falls toward the axis, so the partial integrals shrink to zero
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the logarithm grows

options.text: The curve approaches the horizontal line, so the partial integrals converge to that height
options.misconception: reads a slowly rising curve as approaching its asymptote

options.text: The curve rises without bound, so the partial integrals lack a finite limit and the integral diverges
The curve oscillates, so the partial integrals alternate around a limit
options.misconception: imagines oscillation in a monotone function

questions.explanation: The partial integrals of 1 over x from 1 to b are ln b, and the sketch shows them rising without bound, slowly but inexorably. A monotone unbounded curve means the improper integral diverges.
questions.hint: A monotone curve that never levels off means divergence.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: A convergent logarithmic integral
questions.learningObjective: Compute a partial integral that displays the slow growth of the harmonic integral
questions.stem: A long corrected exercise asks for the partial integral from 1 to 1000 of 1 over x, reported in area units to four decimal places, to show how slowly the divergent harmonic integral grows.
questions.explanation: The partial integral is the natural logarithm of the upper limit, so the integral from 1 to 1000 of 1 over x equals ln 1000 = 6.9077553, which rounds to 6.9078. Even at such a large upper limit the value grows only logarithmically.
questions.hint: The partial integral is the natural logarithm of the upper limit.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Type I integral as a limit
questions.learningObjective: State what must hold for the limit of truncated integrals to define an improper integral
questions.stem: One question asks what must be true of the limit of the truncated integrals for an improper integral over an infinite interval to be defined and to converge. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The integrand must tend to zero, which is enough for the improper integral to converge
options.misconception: believes a vanishing integrand settles the question

options.text: The limit must exist, and an infinite limit may be reported as the value of the integral
options.misconception: accepts an infinite limit as a legitimate value

options.text: The truncated integrals must be bounded, which is enough for the improper integral to converge
options.misconception: believes bounded truncated integrals alone guarantee convergence

options.text: The limit must exist and be a finite number, and then the improper integral equals that number

questions.explanation: An improper integral is the limit of the truncated proper integrals, and it converges only when that limit is a finite real number. Bounded truncation or a vanishing integrand are not sufficient.
questions.hint: The limit must be finite for convergence.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Reciprocal power on an infinite interval
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate an exponential improper integral from a shifted lower limit
questions.stem: A long corrected exercise asks for the improper integral from 1 to infinity of e^(-x) dx. Compute the value to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: The truncated integral from 1 to b is e^(-1) - e^(-b), and its limit as b grows is e^(-1) = 0.3678794, which rounds to 0.3679. The exponential decays fast enough for the tail area to be finite.
questions.hint: Evaluate the truncated integral and then take the limit.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Type II integral at an interior singularity
questions.learningObjective: Correct the claim that an endpoint magnitude argument settles an integral with an interior singularity
questions.stem: A student writes that the integral from 0 to 2 of 1 over (x-1) must be zero because the antiderivative ln of the absolute value has the same magnitude at both endpoints. Write an explanation that corrects the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: The antiderivative ln|x-1| is not continuous across x = 1, so the difference of its endpoint values is meaningless here. The integral has to be split at x = 1 into two one-sided improper integrals: the left piece, with the lower limit approaching 1 from below, tends to minus infinity, and the right piece tends to plus infinity. Since neither piece has a finite value, the improper integral diverges, and the apparent cancellation of the endpoint magnitudes is exactly the mistake.

questions.explanation: The antiderivative ln of the absolute value has different one-sided behaviours at the interior singularity, so endpoint values cannot be differenced. Each one-sided piece diverges, so the integral diverges.
questions.hint: The antiderivative is discontinuous at the singularity.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Condition on a reciprocal-power exponent
questions.learningObjective: Identify the singularity of a rational integrand and the behaviour of each piece
questions.stem: A final exercise about the integral from 0 to 4 of 1 over (x-2) dx asks where to split the integral and how each resulting piece behaves.

options.text: The integrand blows up at x = 2, so split there; both one-sided pieces tend to +infinity, so it diverges upward
options.misconception: gets the sign of the right-hand piece wrong

options.text: The integrand blows up at x = 2, so split there; the left piece tends to -infinity and the right to +infinity
The integrand is finite at x = 2, so no split is needed and the antiderivative formula applies
options.misconception: denies the singularity visible in the integrand

options.text: The integrand blows up at x = 2, but the two infinite pieces cancel, so the integral equals zero
options.misconception: cancels two infinite quantities to claim a finite value

questions.explanation: The singularity at x = 2 forces a split, and ln of the absolute value tends to -infinity from the left and +infinity from the right. Neither piece is finite, so the integral diverges and the infinities cannot be cancelled.
questions.hint: Use the antiderivative ln of the absolute value on each side.
